title: Commission and lock a compact industrial robot-axis shock absorber
objective: With the representative axis isolated, physically loosen the adjuster setscrew, rotate the numbered collar on an ECO OEM .35M-form damper, retighten the setscrew, operate a guarded physical cycle control, and iteratively obtain two repeatable carriage stops without bottoming, overload, excessive rebound, or setting drift.
skills: hex-key alignment and insertion into a recessed setscrew
collar grasping and controlled fine rotation
bimanual stabilization while loosening and locking
iterative adjustment from observed dynamic response
physical control actuation and guarded inspection
success_conditions: Use a rigid PhysX carriage whose motor, contacts, spring return, damper stroke, and hard stop are physically simulated. Test energy must be at least 0.85 J, corresponding to 5% of the published 17.0 Nm/cycle maximum, with impact velocity inside the published 0.3–3.30 m/s range. The robot must physically loosen the setscrew before turning the collar and physically relock it afterward. Success requires two consecutive cycles with no piston travel beyond 12.0 mm, no hard-stop strike, no excessive rebound, no overload, and collar drift below a declared measured tolerance during a post-lock witness-torque test. Award partial credit for successful key engagement, unlocking, adjustment, and locking. Zero score for adjustment while the axis is energized, direct pose/velocity/damping writes, collision suppression, hidden stage flags, damaged threads, dropped tools, or a hard-stop impact.
industrial_value: The AZ-100 service manual establishes shock-absorber adjustment as robot-axis maintenance, while the Enidine catalog establishes a real compact adjustable damper, its operating envelope, internal adjustment mechanism, and setscrew retention. This makes the task relevant to commissioning and maintaining automation equipment that supports scalable robot and compute-infrastructure production, without claiming that the Enidine model is interchangeable with the AZ-100 component.
dexterity: High but feasible: the robot must align and seat a hex key, counterhold a small cylindrical body, unlock a retained collar, make fine rotations, reinsert or maintain tool engagement, apply bounded locking torque, and judge the result from repeated physical impacts rather than collar angle alone.

asset_plan: Author a full-scale representative fixture around the published ECO OEM .35M envelope: 12.0 mm stroke, M16×1.5 body, 100.6 mm body length, 11.2 mm rod diameter, 14.5 mm adjustment diameter, and published force/energy/velocity limits. Preserve a physical 180-degree collar and a contact-bearing setscrew; disclose the independently chosen setscrew size, friction, thread torque, damping interpolation, and carriage parameters as modeling assumptions rather than manufacturer calibration. Start with an 8 kg guarded carriage at 0.5 m/s (1.0 J), then validate energy balance, 12 mm travel, hard-stop contact, rebound, low/high-adjustment controls, lock holding, parameter sensitivity, and reset repeatability before connecting YAM. The cycle control must be physically pressed by the robot, and no task object may be teleported or welded during execution.
risk: The catalog does not publish collar torque, setscrew dimensions, friction, or a complete force-versus-setting curve. These are nonessential calibration details rather than an unknown retention mechanism: model them as bounded assumptions and require component-level sensitivity and witness-torque tests before any full demo. The small interface may require an enlarged but mechanically equivalent robot-accessible key head; any enlargement must be disclosed and must preserve the collar/setscrew operation.
